# Overview

`qtlPCABrowser()` launches a Shiny application that runs PCA on the
per-covariate t-statistics produced by
[`qtlRegressionStats()`](regressionStats.html) for a set of SNP-gene pairs,
and lets you explore the result interactively:

- a **PCA scatter** tab (`plotly`) with selectable PC axes; hovering over a
  point shows a beeswarm of that pair's gene expression by genotype, in the
  panel to the right, optionally colored by a sample-level covariate,
- a **PC pairs** tab, a base-R `pairs()` plot of the first five PCs.

Because each row of the t-statistic matrix is one SNP-gene pair and each
column is one covariate term, PC1/PC2 of this matrix summarize how pairs
differ in the *pattern* of covariate effects driving their association --
useful for spotting pairs whose signal is dominated by a batch or
population effect rather than genotype.

```{r loaddata, message=FALSE}
library(tQTLExperiment)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
```

# Two ways to launch it

`qtlPCABrowser()` has two modes, selected by which argument you supply.

## Gene-symbol mode (`tqe` only)

Supply just a `tQTLExperiment` with gene symbols already added
(`addGeneSymbols()`). The app shows a gene-symbol selector; on "Compute
regression stats/PCA" it calls `qtlRegressionStats(tqe, symbol = ...)` for
the chosen gene, then PCA's the result. Repeat calls for the same gene are
memoised within the Shiny session.

```{r genemode, eval=FALSE}
exdir <- system.file("extdata", package = "tQTLExperiment")
tqe <- tQTLExperiment(
    plinkPrefix = file.path(exdir, "chr22-n100"),
    phenoFile   = file.path(exdir, "mean-pheno-n100.bed"),
    covFile     = file.path(exdir, "cov-n100-tqtl.tsv"),
    genome      = "hg38"
)
tqe <- addGeneSymbols(tqe)
qtlPCABrowser(tqe)
```

This mode is the right default when you don't yet know which genes are
interesting: compute on demand, gene by gene.

## Pre-computed mode (`res` supplied)

If you already have a wide `qtlRegressionStats()` result -- for instance
for every gene in a region, computed ahead of time and possibly in
parallel -- pass it as `res`; the gene-symbol selector is skipped and the
app opens directly on the combined PCA.

```{r precomp, eval=FALSE}
symbols <- na.omit(unique(mcols(rowRanges(tqe))[["gene_name"]]))
res_list <- lapply(symbols, function(s)
    tryCatch(qtlRegressionStats(tqe, symbol = s), error = function(e) NULL))
res_all <- do.call(rbind, res_list)
qtlPCABrowser(res_all, tqe = tqe)
```

`res` must contain `phenotype_id` and `variant_id` columns (the wide,
`t_only = TRUE` shape `qtlRegressionStats()` returns by default).

# What happens to the t-statistic columns

Before PCA, `qtlPCABrowser()` runs `collapseFactorTstats()` on `res` (or on
each gene's freshly computed result), using the `collapse_patterns`
argument -- by default tuned for the MAGE dataset's `factor_batch_*` and
`population*` dummy columns. This keeps a factor with many levels from
dominating the PCA the way `qtlRegressionStats()` alone would, since it
would otherwise contribute one raw t-statistic column per level. Pass your
own `collapse_patterns` list if your covariates use different names -- see
`?collapseFactorTstats`.

```{r collapsedemo, eval=FALSE}
qtlPCABrowser(
    tqe,
    collapse_patterns = list(
        site = "^t\\.site",
        sex  = "^t\\.sex"
    )
)
```

PCA itself is `stats::prcomp()` on the resulting t-statistic matrix,
centered but not scaled (`center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE`), so columns with
naturally larger t-statistics -- typically genotype -- dominate the leading
PCs, which is usually the point.

# Interpreting the scatter-plus-beeswarm view

Hovering a point in the PCA scatter plot identifies a SNP-gene pair, whose
genotype effect is then drawn in the beeswarm panel using the same data
extraction as [`plotGenotypeEffect()`](../reference/plotGenotypeEffect.html):
genotype (0/1/2 alternate alleles) on the x-axis, phenotype value on the
y-axis. The "Color beeswarm by" selector reconstructs the original factor
levels from the covariate dummy columns (e.g. `batch`, `population`) plus
any remaining numeric covariates, so you can immediately check whether an
outlying PCA point corresponds to a pair whose apparent effect is really
driven by one covariate level rather than genotype.
